items.title: .GetAwaiter().GetResult() blocks on async work
items.body:
**Key: it blocks on async work, which deadlocks wherever a synchronization context exists.**

`DispatchDomainEvents` is an `async` method. On the synchronous `SavingChanges` path, the code calls it and then `.GetAwaiter().GetResult()`, which makes the current thread wait until the async work finishes. This is called "sync over async". In environments with a *synchronization context* (for example older ASP.NET or desktop UI apps), the async work wants to continue on the very thread that is now blocked waiting for it, so both wait forever: a deadlock. Modern ASP.NET Core has no such context, which is why ADR-009 calls it harmless here but a landmine elsewhere.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Moves the save to a new thread*: `GetResult()` blocks the current thread; it does not move work.
- *Swallows exceptions*: `GetResult()` rethrows the task's exception.
- *Dispatches twice*: each save goes through one of the two overrides, not both.

excerpts.quote: public override InterceptionResult<int> SavingChanges(DbContextEventData eventData, InterceptionResult<int> result) { DispatchDomainEvents(eventData.Context).GetAwaiter().GetResult();
blocks on async work via `.GetAwaiter().GetResult()` on the synchronous save path — harmless under modern ASP.NET Core's lack of a synchronization context, a deadlock elsewhere.

items.title: A field the client must not set needs its own request DTO
items.body:
**Key: give that endpoint a real request DTO and keep direct binding for the others.**

In this template the JSON body binds straight into the Application command; there is no separate request type. That is fine while every command field is something the client may set. A server-controlled field breaks the assumption: a client could put a value for it in the body (mass-assignment, also called over-posting). The guide's advice is a question to ask for each new field, "should the client be allowed to set this?", and when the answer is no, that endpoint needs a real request DTO.

Why the others are wrong:
- *A DTO and mapper in front of every command*: the guide keeps the convention and fixes only the endpoint that needs it.
- *A validator rule that rejects the field*: the guide prescribes a request DTO, because nothing structural stops the binding.
- *Over-posting stays theoretical*: the guide calls it a real vulnerability.

excerpts.quote: If no, the direct-bind convention is working against you and you need a real request DTO for that endpoint.
that's mass-assignment / over-posting, and it's a real vulnerability, not a theoretical one.

items.title: Every authenticated request pays a database lookup for a log label
items.body:
**Key: a database lookup of the username for log labels in two behaviours.**

`LoggingBehaviour` and `PerformanceBehaviour` both want to write a readable user name in their log lines. They only have the user id, so each queries the database to turn the id into a username. Every request from a logged-in user therefore makes a database round trip just for logging. ADR-003 lists this under negative consequences as "I/O in the pipeline".

Why the others are wrong:
- *Each behaviour opens its own transaction*: behaviours do not open transactions.
- *Validated twice*: `ValidationBehaviour` runs once per request.
- *The pipeline serialises requests*: behaviours wrap each request separately; nothing makes requests wait for each other.

excerpts.quote: `LoggingBehaviour` and `PerformanceBehaviour` each do a DB query to turn a user id into a username
so *every authenticated request* pays a round trip for a log label.

items.title: MediatR behaviours: wrappers around every request
items.body:
In this template a web endpoint does not call business code directly. It sends a request object (a command or query) through MediatR, which finds its handler. Before the handler runs, the request passes through a chain of *behaviours*. Each behaviour is a small class that can do something before and after calling `next()`, like layers of an onion around the handler.

The behaviours are registered in `Application/DependencyInjection.cs`, and ADR-003 says the registration order is deliberate. Look up in the ADR or the MediatR documentation how registration order turns into execution order, then read the five `AddOpenRequestPreProcessor`/`AddOpenBehavior` lines and draw the onion yourself.

For each behaviour, write down which other layers end up inside it, what it does before and after `next()`, and what it prevents from running if it throws. Then read each behaviour's code for any work it does on every request. ADR-003 explains the choice and lists its costs.

excerpts.quote: cfg.AddOpenRequestPreProcessor(typeof(LoggingBehaviour<>)); cfg.AddOpenBehavior(typeof(UnhandledExceptionBehaviour<,>));
Wrap every MediatR request in a pipeline of `IPipelineBehavior` implementations, registered — and therefore executed — in a deliberate order.

readMore.why: The positive and negative consequences of the pipeline design.

items.title: An unsupported colour becomes a 500, not a 400
items.body:
**Key: 500, because the domain exception is not mapped like validation failures.**

There is no FluentValidation rule for colour, so the request passes layer 3. The value reaches the domain, where `Colour.From` throws `UnsupportedColourException` (layer 4). The exception handler maps validation exceptions to a 400 `ValidationProblemDetails`, but nothing maps this domain exception, so it becomes a generic 500. The guide calls it a gap: the same kind of bad input gets a different error contract depending on which layer catches it. Its suggested fix is both a validator rule and an exception mapping.

Why the others are wrong:
- *400 like any invalid field*: only validator failures are mapped to 400.
- *422 after validation passes*: no mapping produces 422.
- *200 with a default colour*: `Colour.From` throws; it does not substitute.

excerpts.quote: Send colour `"#BADBAD"` and `UnsupportedColourException` becomes a **500**, not a 400 — domain invariant violations and validation failures produce different contracts.
[Colour.From](../../src/Domain/ValueObjects/Colour.cs#L5-L15) throws `UnsupportedColourException`

items.title: Parallelizing this suite would cause the cross-talk
items.body:
**Key: it would cause the cross-talk, so first remove the static user fields in TestApp.**

`TestApp` stores the current test user in `private static` fields (`_userId`, `_roles`). Static fields are shared by the whole process, so two tests running at the same time would overwrite each other's identity. Respawn's reset between tests also assumes only one test uses the database at a time. That is why the suite runs serially. Turning on `[Parallelizable]` would create exactly the cross-talk the colleague thinks they are fixing. The guide's order of work: remove the statics first.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Statics scoped to each test's thread*: static fields are process-global.
- *Respawn already isolates each test*: its reset assumes one test at a time.
- *A database per test, keeping the statics*: the shared identity would still collide; the statics have to go first.

excerpts.quote: Static process-global state means **two tests running at once would stomp on each other's identity.**
The right fix is to remove the statics first.

items.title: Start here: the Clean Architecture template, read through its guides
items.body:
This pack uses Jason Taylor's Clean Architecture template for .NET: a small todo-list app whose real subject is the architecture (Domain, Application, Infrastructure and Web layers, MediatR, FluentValidation, EF Core). The `fabledocs` folders are a training course built on it, and `fabledocs3` holds short Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) that explain why things are built the way they are.

Suggested reading order for this pack:

1. `CleanArchitecture/fabledocs/README.md`: what the template is, and its caveat that it is a template with deliberate gaps.
2. `fabledocs/03-architecture-and-patterns/03-validation-auth-and-permissions.md`: the validation layers, authentication and authorization.
3. `fabledocs3/adr-003-behaviour-pipeline.md`: the ordered MediatR pipeline.
4. `fabledocs3/adr-009-in-process-precommit-domain-events.md`: when domain events are published, and the risks.
5. `fabledocs2/03-data-access.md` and `fabledocs/03-architecture-and-patterns/04-side-effects-async-and-reliability.md` for background.

Open each linked source file as you go; the guides cite exact lines. For every guarantee a guide describes, ask what the code would have to record or check to make it true, and then look for that record or check.

excerpts.quote: The sample domain is deliberately small — todo lists and todo items — so the architecture is the star.
**One caveat you must internalize early:** this repo is a *template*.

readMore.why: The index of the ten architecture decision records.
The weekend path: run it, trace two flows, make one safe change.

items.title: Logged in is not the same as allowed: the missing owner check
items.body:
**Key: read or change other users' lists, because nothing records or checks an owner.**

`RequireAuthorization()` only asks "are you logged in?", and `[Authorize]` adds "are you in this role?". Neither asks "is this todo list *yours*?". TodoList has no owner column, queries are not filtered by user, and handlers do not check ownership before changing a row. So any logged-in user can read, edit or delete another user's lists by trying ids 1, 2, 3... This class of bug is IDOR, or broken object-level authorization.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Writes filtered by CreatedBy*: `CreatedBy` is only an audit field; no handler filters on it.
- *A per-user global filter on items*: there is no such filter.
- *RequireAuthorization scopes every query*: it checks authentication, not ownership.

excerpts.quote: Authorization here answers *authenticated?* and *in role?* — never *"is this todo list yours?"* There is no ownership column on TodoList (only audit fields)
Any authenticated user can read, modify, or delete any other user's data by iterating small integer IDs.

readMore.why: The five checks a senior makes, in order, to rule out IDOR.

items.title: Pre-commit dispatch can send a ghost notification
items.body:
**Key: a ghost notification: the email left even though the change never committed.**

The interceptor publishes events while EF is *saving changes*, before the database commit. The handler runs then and sends the email. If the save fails afterwards, the database rolls back, but an email that has been sent cannot be called back. The user is told about a change that does not exist. ADR-009 lists this first among the negative consequences: external side effects escape the transaction.

Why the others are wrong:
- *The save is retried*: nothing retries the save.
- *The email is queued in the transaction*: that would be an outbox, which is not implemented.
- *Published again after a retry*: there is no retry, and events are cleared before publishing to prevent re-entrancy.

excerpts.quote: **Pre-commit dispatch means external side effects escape the transaction.** If a handler sends an email and the save then fails, you've sent a ghost notification

items.title: Result for expected failures, exceptions for exceptional ones
items.body:
**Key: whether it is an expected outcome the caller branches on or an exceptional one.**

The pipeline mostly signals errors with typed exceptions that one handler maps to HTTP. But Identity operations return a `Result`, because "the password was too weak" is a normal outcome the caller has to branch on. Not found, not authorized and invalid input are exceptional relative to a handler's happy path, so they throw. For the interview question "exceptions or result types?", the guide's advice is not to pick a side but to say it depends on whether the failure is exceptional or expected.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Identity code versus the app's handlers*: the source of the failure does not decide; its kind does.
- *A 4xx versus a 500*: exceptional failures such as not-found also end up as client errors.
- *Written before or after Result became the default*: Result was rejected as the default.

excerpts.quote: Domain-contract violations throw; user-facing expected failures return results.
it depends on whether the failure is exceptional or expected

items.title: Renaming an endpoint method renames the generated client method
items.body:
**Key: the operationId comes from the method name, so both SPAs get a renamed client method.**

When an endpoint is registered, the code calls `.WithName(handler.Method.Name)`, and that name becomes the OpenAPI `operationId`. NSwag turns the operationId into the generated TypeScript method, so the C# method `GetTodoLists` becomes `getTodoLists()` in both frontends. Rename the C# method and the generated method gets a new name, while every call site in the SPAs still uses the old one. The guide calls this a breaking API change whose blast radius is invisible from the method itself.

Why the others are wrong:
- *The backend stops compiling*: in the guide's incident the backend CI was green; it was the frontend build that failed.
- *Only server log labels change*: both SPAs and any external OpenAPI consumer are affected.
- *NSwag names client methods from route and verb*: the guide shows the method name flowing straight into the client method name.

excerpts.quote: we derive its name — which becomes the OpenAPI `operationId` — from the **handler method's name**.
The backend CI was green (C# compiles fine).

items.title: Suppressing the pending-changes warning hides schema drift
items.body:
**Key: schema drift goes unseen, as the alarm that the model diverged has been silenced.**

The template builds its schema with `EnsureCreated` and has no migrations. EF Core normally warns when the model has pending changes that no migration captures; line 33 of `Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs` turns that warning off, so nothing tells you the model has moved away from what a migration would produce. ADR-010 lists this among its negative consequences, and the interview answer says a production fork should un-suppress the warning so drift is visible again.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Seeding stops being idempotent*: seeding is guarded so it can safely re-run.
- *Migrations apply silently*: there are no migrations at all.
- *Only SQLite tolerates it*: one model targets SQLite, PostgreSQL and SQL Server behind switches.

excerpts.quote: **Schema drift is invisible** because the pending-changes warning is suppressed
guarded so seeding is idempotent

items.title: The outbox becomes necessary once a handler does external I/O
items.body:
**Key: as soon as a handler performs external I/O such as sending email.**

A *transactional outbox* saves events in the same database transaction as the change, and a background worker delivers them afterwards with retries. It exists to make side effects *outside* the database reliable. Today the only event handler writes a log line, so the risks of in-process dispatch are latent. ADR-009 names the moment that changes: "the moment a handler does I/O", such as sending an email or calling another service.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Once an event has two handlers*: the number of handlers does not change the reliability problem.
- *In-process dispatch already guarantees at-least-once*: ADR-009 says the opposite: "at-most-once, in-process, lost on crash".
- *When moving from SQLite to SQL Server*: the database engine is unrelated to where side effects happen.

excerpts.quote: The industry-standard answer for *reliable external* side effects. Not implemented — appropriate given every current handler only logs, but it's the upgrade path the moment a handler does I/O.
There is no delivery guarantee beyond at-most-once, in-process, lost on crash.

items.title: Two role attributes OR together in this behaviour
items.body:
**Key: authorized: one flag spans all attributes, so they OR together.**

Trace the loop. `authorized` starts as `false`, once, before the outer `foreach`. First attribute, roles "A": the user is not in A, so nothing changes. Second attribute, roles "B": the user is in B, so `authorized = true`. After the loop, `if (!authorized)` is false, so no exception. One match anywhere is enough. ASP.NET Core's own `[Authorize]` attributes work the other way: each attribute must be satisfied.

Note: the guide's paragraph on line 32 first says role attributes "AND together", then tells you to check that claim yourself; its drill 2 answer and the code both say OR.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Forbidden, every attribute must match*: that is ASP.NET Core's rule, not this loop's.
- *Rejected at startup*: nothing validates attributes at startup.
- *Only the first attribute counts*: the loop visits every attribute with roles.

excerpts.quote: var authorized = false; foreach (var roles in authorizeAttributesWithRoles.Select(a => a.Roles.Split(','))) { foreach (var role in roles) { var isInRole = _user.Roles?.Any(x => role == x)??false; if (isInRole) { authorized = true;
(Answer: yes — one flag across all attributes, so attributes OR together, unlike ASP.NET Core's AND semantics.

items.title: The id check is transport logic, and endpoint logic tends to grow
items.body:
**Key: it is transport logic about URL versus body, and endpoints may accrete more logic.**

`UpdateTodoItem` compares the `id` from the route with `command.Id` from the body and returns `BadRequest()` if they differ. The author keeps that in the endpoint because it is about the relationship between the URL and the payload, an HTTP idea the handler should not need to know about. The risk the author watches is growth: today an id check, next a null check, then a "quick" business rule, until endpoints hold logic the handlers do not know about and the tests do not cover.

Why the others are wrong:
- *A business rule the handler lacks*: the guide classifies it as transport logic, not business logic.
- *A 404 leaking which ids exist*: the check returns 400, and the risk named is creeping endpoint logic.
- *It needs the signed-in user*: it compares two ids and uses no identity at all.

excerpts.quote: it's about the relationship between the URL and the payload, which is an HTTP idea the handler shouldn't need to know exists.
it's the kind of thing that, uncontested, grows — next it's a null check, then a "quick" business rule

items.title: Validation reports every failure in a single response
items.body:
**Key: one 400 listing all three, gathered by the validation behaviour before one throw.**

`ValidationBehaviour` is a MediatR pipeline stage. It runs every validator for the request, collects every failure, and throws a single `ValidationException` with a dictionary from property name to messages. The exception handler turns that into one 400 `ValidationProblemDetails` response. So the client sees every problem with its input at once instead of fixing one field per round trip, which the guide lists as the incident this design prevented.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Only the first failure*: the behaviour collects all failures before throwing.
- *Gathered by the endpoint from model binding*: the aggregation happens in the pipeline behaviour, not in the endpoint.
- *One 400 per failing field*: there is one exception and therefore one response.

excerpts.quote: aggregates *all* failures, and throws a single `ValidationException` carrying a `PropertyName → messages[]` dictionary.
So a client gets *every* problem with their input at once, not one-at-a-time.

items.title: What pre-commit dispatch buys: same-context writes commit together
items.body:
**Key: handlers writing to the same DbContext commit atomically with the trigger.**

Because events are published during `SaveChanges`, before the commit, a handler that changes other rows through the *same* `DbContext` adds those changes to the same save. The trigger and the handler's writes then commit or fail together: no "dual write" where one succeeds and the other does not. ADR-009 says this is why the authors chose before-commit over after-commit dispatch.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Events survive a crash*: events live in memory; ADR-009 says they are "lost on crash".
- *Emails delivered exactly once*: pre-commit dispatch is exactly what causes ghost emails.
- *Handlers run on a background thread*: `Publish` awaits handlers inline on the user's request.

excerpts.quote: A handler that writes to the *same* `DbContext` joins the same `SaveChanges` and commits atomically with the trigger — no dual-write for the common in-DB case.
the authors chose before-commit for atomicity with same-context handler writes.

items.title: Behaviours work without HTTP; filters and middleware do not
items.body:
**Key: they must also apply to non-HTTP entry points, such as tests sending through ISender.**

MVC filters and middleware run as part of handling an HTTP request. A MediatR behaviour runs whenever a request is sent through MediatR, however it got there. Tests send requests directly with `ISender`, and a future queue consumer would too. ADR-003 points to the functional test that denies an anonymous user: it proves authorization works "with zero HTTP involved", which is only possible because it is a behaviour.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Behaviours are faster*: speed is not the reason the ADR gives.
- *Middleware runs after the handler*: middleware runs before and after the endpoint; timing is not the issue.
- *Filters cannot read the body*: the ADR's argument is about transport independence.

excerpts.quote: Would tie cross-cutting logic to the HTTP transport — but these concerns are *application* concerns that must also apply to non-HTTP entry points (tests via `ISender`, a future queue consumer).

items.title: The innermost behaviour times only the handler
items.body:
**Key: only the handler itself.**

`PerformanceBehaviour` is registered last, so it is the layer closest to the handler. It starts its stopwatch, calls `next()` (which is the handler), and stops the stopwatch when `next()` returns. Everything outside it (exception logging, authorization, validation) has already run before it starts, so none of that time is counted. ADR-003 says this is why it is innermost.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Only the EF interceptors*: interceptors run inside the handler's database calls; they are part of the handler's time, not all of it.
- *The whole HTTP request*: model binding and routing happen before MediatR is even called.
- *Authorization plus validation, not the handler*: those run outside it.

excerpts.quote: performance timing is innermost so it measures only the handler.
cfg.AddOpenBehavior(typeof(PerformanceBehaviour<,>));

items.title: No suite exercises the todo endpoints' HTTP behaviour
items.body:
**Key: both suites miss it, as functional tests enter below it and Todo.feature is missing.**

The id-consistency check lives in `TodoItems.cs`, an endpoint. Functional tests send commands through `ISender`, which sits below the endpoints, so routing, binding, status codes and that check never run there. The acceptance suite drives a real browser, but it only has features for Home, Counter, Weather and Login; there is no `Todo.feature`. The guide says breaking the check would leave every test green, and calls adding a `Todo.feature` acceptance test the highest-value test work in the repo.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Application.FunctionalTests*: they enter at `ISender`, so the endpoint code never runs.
- *Web.AcceptanceTests*: no feature covers the todo screens.
- *Domain.UnitTests*: the check is in the endpoint, not in the TodoItem entity.

excerpts.quote: the todo endpoints' HTTP behavior is tested by *neither* the functional nor the acceptance suite.
the acceptance layer only covers Home/Counter/Weather/Login (there's no `Todo.feature`)

items.title: TodoItemCompletedEvent fires only on false to true
items.body:
**Key: only when Done changes from false to true, inside the setter.**

The `Done` property has a custom setter. It adds the event only `if (value && !_done)`: the new value is true *and* the old value was false. Setting `Done = true` again on an item that is already done adds nothing. Because the rule lives in the setter, every code path that sets `Done` (handlers, seed data, tests) gets the same behaviour; no caller can forget to raise the event.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Every assignment of true*: the `!_done` check stops repeats.
- *Any property change on a completed item*: only the `Done` setter raises this event.
- *A handler calls Publish after SaveChanges*: the entity adds the event; the interceptor publishes it before the commit.

excerpts.quote: if (value && !_done) { AddDomainEvent(new TodoItemCompletedEvent(this)); } _done = value;
adds a `TodoItemCompletedEvent` *only* on the false→true transition, an invariant encoded so no call site can forget it.

items.title: Domain events and the SaveChanges seam
items.body:
A *domain event* is a message an entity raises to say "something happened" (here: a todo item was completed), so other code can react without the entity knowing who listens. In this template the entity only adds the event to a list. Nothing is sent yet.

The sending happens in an EF Core *interceptor*: code that EF calls around `SaveChanges`. `DispatchDomainEventsInterceptor` overrides both the asynchronous and the synchronous "saving changes" hooks and publishes the collected events through MediatR.

The key question for this part of the pack is *timing*. "Saving changes" runs before the database commit. Before the quizzes, read ADR-009's Decision and Alternatives, and write down: what can go wrong if a handler does something outside the database, and what can go wrong if events are published after the commit instead?

excerpts.quote: The domain needs to signal that something happened ("a todo item was completed") so other code can react without the trigger knowing who's listening.
public override async ValueTask<InterceptionResult<int>> SavingChangesAsync(DbContextEventData eventData, InterceptionResult<int> result, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)

readMore.why: Side effects, async and reliability across the codebase.

items.title: Place each test at the lowest layer that can see the failure
items.body:
**Key: use the lowest layer that can still observe the failure you actually fear.**

The four test projects each enter the system at a different seam, and each is blind to something another one catches. So the question for a new test is not "which layer is best?" but "which failure am I afraid of, and what is the lowest layer that can actually see it?" The guide states the tradeoff in one line: push a fear down a layer and the test gets faster but fictional; push it up and it gets real but slow and vague.

Why the others are wrong:
- *The highest layer*: real, but slow, and a full-stack failure says little about where it broke.
- *The fastest layer*: if that layer cannot see the failure, the test is fictional.
- *Each layer at once*: the rule picks one layer per fear; the layers complement each other rather than duplicate.

excerpts.quote: **test at the lowest layer that can observe the failure you actually fear.**
Push a fear down a layer and it's faster but fictional; push it up and it's real but slow and vague.

items.title: Why hand-written operation ids were rejected as the default
items.body:
**Key: renames tend to leave the literal stale, so code and contract silently disagree.**

The alternative to deriving the name was to write `.WithName("GetTodoLists")` by hand on every endpoint. The author rejected it because it is boilerplate that drifts: someone renames the method, forgets the string, and nothing complains. Deriving the name from the method keeps code and contract in lockstep by construction. The guide is honest that this trades one risk for another, and says that for a public-facing API it would pin explicit ids after all.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Pinned ids suit internal APIs only*: the guide says the opposite; a public-facing API is where it would pin them.
- *NSwag ignores literal names*: nothing in the guide says so; explicit ids are presented as a working option.
- *A reflection lookup per request*: performance is never the reason given.

excerpts.quote: I rejected it because it's boilerplate that drifts: people forget to update the string when they rename the method, and now your code and your contract disagree silently.
If I were doing it again for a public-facing API, I'd pin explicit operation IDs and accept the drift risk

items.title: Why rollback-per-test was rejected for the functional suite
items.body:
**Key: it breaks once a handler commits its own transaction, which every handler does.**

Wrapping each test in a transaction and rolling it back at the end only isolates tests while the code under test leaves that transaction open. In this codebase every handler saves and commits its own work, so a rollback around the test cannot undo it. ADR-008 chose Respawn instead, which resets the data (not the schema) between tests.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Slower, each test booting a container*: that is the reason container-per-test isolation was rejected.
- *Relies on the in-memory provider*: that describes the mocked or in-memory alternative, rejected because it accepts queries the real provider cannot translate.
- *Clashes with the static user fields*: the statics are the reason the suite cannot run in parallel, a separate consequence.

excerpts.quote: Breaks the moment code under test commits its own transaction (which every handler does).
**Container-per-test isolation.** Cleaner isolation, far slower.

items.title: FluentValidation is the contract authority, but uniqueness races
items.body:
**Key: FluentValidation in the pipeline; its uniqueness check races because nothing locks.**

The guide's table marks layer 3, FluentValidation run by `ValidationBehaviour`, as "the contract authority": it holds every rule, reports all errors at once, and can check the database (`MustAsync(BeUniqueTitle)`). Its weakness is cross-row rules. "Is this title unique?" is checked, then the insert happens later, with no lock in between. Two requests with the same title can both pass the check and both insert.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Domain invariants*: the table calls them the "last line", and their weakness is surfacing as 500s, not racing.
- *UI hints*: easily bypassed, but the table does not call them the authority.
- *Model binding*: it checks JSON shape only and is not the authority either.

excerpts.quote: | 3. FluentValidation via pipeline | **The contract authority** — every rule, aggregated errors, async DB checks
racy for cross-row rules (no lock)

items.title: A space after the comma creates a role that never matches
items.body:
**Key: a 403, as splitting without Trim leaves a role named " User" that never matches.**

`AuthorizationBehaviour` splits the roles string with `Split(',')` and does not trim the pieces. `"Admin, User"` therefore becomes `"Admin"` and `" User"`, with a leading space. A user whose role is `User` matches neither, so the behaviour treats them as an authenticated user without the required role and throws `ForbiddenAccessException`, which the exception handler maps to 403. The guide calls this latent: no caller in the repo writes such a string, which is why nobody has hit it.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Access granted after trimming*: there is no `Trim()`.
- *A 401*: 401 is for a request with no authenticated user at all; this user is signed in.
- *A startup failure*: nothing checks role strings at startup, which is why the edge has survived.

excerpts.quote: produces a role literally named `" User"`, which will never match anything.
`ForbiddenAccessException` when the user is authenticated but lacks the role/policy

items.title: Every exception that can escape a handler needs an HTTP identity
items.body:
**Key: grep Domain and Application for every Exception subclass and confirm it is mapped.**

In the fork's incident, colour codes from an API integration threw a domain exception that the error mapper did not know, so each one became a 500 and paged people. The guide's lesson is broader than colours: every exception type that can escape a handler needs a deliberate HTTP identity, so periodically grep the Domain and Application layers for `: Exception` and check each one is mapped. An unmapped domain exception is a latent 500.

Why the others are wrong:
- *A catch-all arm that returns 400*: unmapped exceptions becoming 500 is right for genuinely unexpected errors such as a `NullReferenceException`.
- *Route all clients through the UI*: the API is the contract; the UI is just one client.
- *Swap domain exceptions for Result*: the guide keeps throwing for domain-contract violations.

excerpts.quote: Periodically grep your Domain and Application layers for `: Exception` and check each one is mapped.
a `NullReferenceException` *should* be a 500

items.title: Further reading: API design, testing strategy and the error contract
items.body:
The later items in this pack draw on three chapters of `CleanArchitecture/fabledocs2` and on four more ADRs in `fabledocs3`. Each chapter is short and follows the same shape: what the code does, the hardest decisions with the alternative the author rejected, an incident, and "three questions before you move on". Try those three questions yourself before the quizzes.

1. `fabledocs2/02-api-design.md`: how the Minimal API endpoints are organised and how the OpenAPI document is produced, plus three design decisions and what each one costs.
2. `fabledocs2/04-testing-strategy.md`: a table of the four test projects, then the decisions behind the functional test suite.
3. `fabledocs2/05-error-handling.md`: how exceptions become HTTP responses, and the gaps the author admits to.
4. `fabledocs3/adr-004`, `adr-007`, `adr-008` and `adr-010`: the same kind of decisions written as Architecture Decision Records, each listing the rejected alternatives. `fabledocs3/interview-translation.md` turns every ADR into a spoken interview answer.

For each decision, write down what was rejected, why, and which failure mode the author tells you to watch for. Open the linked code as you go.

excerpts.quote: The HTTP surface is built on **Minimal APIs**, organized as one class per resource group.
Four layers, each entering the system at a different seam:

items.title: Authorization runs before validation so errors cannot leak
items.body:
**Key: anonymous callers never get validation feedback that could leak which resources exist.**

Validators can do database checks, such as "is this title already taken?" or "does this list exist?". If validation ran first, someone who is not allowed in at all could send requests and read the validation messages to learn about data they should never see. Running `AuthorizationBehaviour` before `ValidationBehaviour` means an unauthorized caller is stopped before any validator says anything. ADR-003 calls this order "load-bearing".

Why the others are wrong:
- *Validation errors logged with the user's name*: logging is a separate pre-processor; the order of these two is not about logs.
- *Performance timing excludes authorization*: that is why `PerformanceBehaviour` is innermost, a different point.
- *Validators may assume ids belong to the caller*: nothing checks ownership at all, as the guide stresses.

excerpts.quote: authorization runs before validation so anonymous callers don't get validation feedback that could leak which resources exist
cfg.AddOpenBehavior(typeof(AuthorizationBehaviour<,>)); cfg.AddOpenBehavior(typeof(ValidationBehaviour<,>));

items.title: The in-memory double passed and a latency alarm fired
items.body:
**Key: as a production latency alarm, after the in-memory double had passed the tests.**

The handler used a LINQ filter that the real EF provider could not turn into SQL. The in-memory test double did not care: it ran the filter in memory and every test passed. In production the query either threw a translation exception or, on an older EF version, quietly loaded the whole table and filtered it in memory. Nobody saw a red test; the first sign was a latency alarm. This incident is why the functional suite now runs against a real database.

Why the others are wrong:
- *A CI failure*: the in-memory provider accepted the query, so CI stayed green.
- *A constraint violation from the mock*: mocked and in-memory contexts ignore constraints rather than add them.
- *A code review comment*: the guide says the first sign came from production latency.

excerpts.quote: The first sign was a latency alarm, not a test failure, because *the tests couldn't see it.*
Against the in-memory test double it evaluated client-side and passed every test.
